A cycloid is the curve traced by a point on the rim of a circle as it rolls along a straight line without slipping. It's one of the most celebrated curves in calculus and mechanics, famous for its elegant mathematical properties and its role in solving classical problems of motion and optimization. The parametric equations are x equals r times t minus sine t, and y equals r times one minus cosine t, where r is the radius of the rolling circle and t is the angle of rotation. The cycloid has cusps—sharp points—at regular intervals where the rolling circle touches the baseline. Between these cusps it forms smooth arches. One of its most remarkable properties is that the arc length of one complete arch equals exactly eight r, or eight times the radius—a beautiful exact result discovered in the seventeenth century. The cycloid is the brachistochrone curve, the path of fastest descent. A ball rolling down a cycloid reaches the bottom faster than rolling down any other curve. It also has the tautochrone property: a ball takes the same time to reach the bottom of a cycloid regardless of where it starts on the curve. The area under one arch equals three pi r squared, exactly three times the area of the generating circle. Galileo conjectured about the cycloid. Then Pascal, Newton, and Leibniz all studied it intensely, making it a proving ground for early calculus.
